text: What's your opinion on 3rd verses in pop songs/Why do you think they went away? However, I noticed around the mid to late 2000's that VCVCBC became the structure used by the vast majority of the pop industry. If the change had came later on (like in the 2010s) I would have probably blamed it on songs being generally shorter. But the tides turned much earlier than that. Fans of... stuff in general... seem to be of two camps; 1) those wanting/demanding change/development and 2) those wanting more of the same old familiar thing. I think it's also to do with what a band gets their fanbase accustomed to... a band like Radiohead, for example, is fairly forward-moving, not really rehashing what they'd already done really, always experimenting... and fans have come to expect that... While other bands maybe did somewhat the same thing for 2-3 albums and then fans continue to want more of that and actually get upset if they deviate too much. So it can go either way I guess. If anything, it's the exception, that fans want more of the same, and Dinosaur Jr. seems to fall in that camp- they seem exempt from any such criticism that they might've stagnated, frankly, because they're genuinely just too fucking cool. But also, how far can what they are really be taken? I don't think sonic experimentation quite like that is their niche, and that it's okay for them to stay in their wheelhouse. text: The long instrumental outro on “People Make the World Go Round” might be the real heart of the song The long version of “People Make the World Go Round” has a whole second half, and I think it’s the best part https://youtu.be/2owZXPyeilc?si=pq2Q5CoSjFxLEqN- Most people probably know “People Make the World Go Round” from the single, which is around 3:30. That version is already great. Thom Bell’s arrangement, Linda Creed’s lyrics, Russell Thompkins Jr. singing in that ridiculous falsetto. But the album version on The Stylistics’ first record is over six minutes long, and right around the point where the single fades out, it just keeps going. And honestly, that’s the part I like the most. The vocals slowly disappear and the whole thing opens up. Bass, drums, congas, all those strange Bell percussion sounds, then guitar and flute drifting in and out. It doesn’t really feel like it’s trying to get anywhere anymore. It just sits in the groove. That part hits me more physically than the first half. It’s hard to explain without sounding slightly ridiculous, but it feels like the song starts breathing differently. The lyrics are actually pretty bleak. Strikes, garbage piling up, pollution, Wall Street losing money. The whole world is dysfunctional. Then the words disappear and the music just keeps going. To me it almost feels like the song is saying: yeah, the world is a mess, but it keeps turning anyway. That’s obviously just my interpretation, but once I started hearing it like that I couldn’t really unhear it. I also found something interesting about the rhythm. I assumed the long instrumental part felt more relaxed because it probably settled into a simple 4/4 groove. Apparently not. The ending vamp has been analysed as alternating between 4/4 and 5/4. Which is kind of funny, because it feels more relaxed even though the meter is actually less regular. Maybe that extra beat is part of why it feels so loose, like the music is constantly hanging around a little longer than you expect. The song also seems to have really appealed to jazz and soul-jazz musicians. Milt Jackson did an eight-minute version, Cleveland Eaton covered it, O’Donel Levy did a great guitar version, and it kept resurfacing later in hip hop and sample culture. I don’t want to claim all those musicians were specifically obsessed with the long Stylistics outro, because there’s no way to know that. But it does feel like there was something in the composition that musicians wanted to stretch out and live inside. Does the long outro change the meaning of the song for you, or does it just feel like an extended groove? And for anyone here who understands the meter better than I do, why does that 4/4 and 5/4 vamp feel so relaxed when the rhythm is actually becoming less regular? If you only know the short version, let the album version keep running past the point where the single would have faded out. That’s where the song really starts for me.
label: Deep Analysis

text: Alexander Bard's many groups Alexander Bard is a Swedish producer and composer whose career in music has spanned for nearly four decades now. Throughout that time, he has created not less than four groups - Army of Lovers, Vaccum, Bodies Without Organs, and Gravitonas - and created a bunch of songs for other groups, such as Crying At The Discoteque for Alcazar. I've heard many songs from all these groups, as they were considerably popular in my country and I personally like most of them. I'm not musically trained at all, but even to me it is clear that the absolute majority of all songs from all these groups pertain to the pop genre. They are easy on the ears, they are often catchy. Not only that, but they all feel like they have been made by the same person or a collection of people. That is, of course, because they are all ultimately made by Bard himself, more or less. The one distinctive feature I can note with all my non-existent musical expertise is that many bridges in his songs feature lyrics, often in a voice distinctly different from the overall sound of the song, or even in a different language. What I don't get is why Bard made so many groups if he continues to pump out the same sort of product through all of them (I'm pretty sure most of the music and lyrics are either his own or approved by him - he seems to be quite egotistical and unlikely to let anyone control the direction). It's not like those groups fell apart - Army of Lovers presented a new banger and a whole album a couple of years ago, Vaccum and Gravitonas apparently still exist. So why so many groups? What's the goal of creating a collection of bands if the music, in its core, stays the same throughout?
label: Deep Analysis

text: Is there an asymmetry to how music critics discuss “simple” and “complex” music? Technical virtuosity and emotional expression are often considered mutually exclusive ideas. I disagree. I would actually posit that prog, jazz, metal, or otherwise maximalist musicians are actually deeply passionate about what they do, often have something unique and profound to say, and are choosing to express themselves with a more advanced form of language, much like poets or playwrights. And rather than attacking the language outright, we should grant these musicians the same grace we extend to three-chord singer-songwriters and ambient synthesists, who are often considered more “honest” artists. What critics call “bloat” can actually serve distinct artistic purposes: Long-form composition can signify a vast journey, literally or metaphorically, and allow the writers ample time for motivic development. Shifting key centers or time signatures can indicate changes in mood or atmosphere. Use of atypical or mixed modes can communicate an unusual or “outsider” perspective. Maximalist arranging can take already large emotions and make them overwhelming. Exceeding the established limitations of musical convention can communicate a deep spiritual transcendence. And yet, often when an artist shows a level of ambition beyond what is “cool,” they are often hit with lazy shorthand words like “overwrought,” “self-indulgent,” or the worst offender “masturbatory.” Conversely, minimalism is granted profundity by default. Restraint is always seen as a sign of “maturity.” Records with a lot of emptier space leave a considerable amount of room for the listener to project their own feelings, increasing a sense of depth that may or may not already be there. This leads to a broader follow-up question: Should paid professional music critics have a better understanding of concepts like composition, arranging, and musicianship? Consider the absurdity of an NFL sportswriter who doesn't know the basic rules and regulations of football; or a food critic who couldn’t distinguish between common cooking methods or ingredients. Why do we allow music critics to feel everything out on vibes instead of insisting that they show a firm understanding about the building blocks of their chosen medium? EDIT: Really appreciate all the thoughtful and insightful replies here, whether we agreed or disagreed. I'm stepping away now, so if you reply to get a final word in, I guess it's the final word. I think I've made my position as clear as it can be in the comments.
label: Philosophical Discussion

text: Lyrics are massively overvalued in how people judge music I think music discussion puts too much weight on lyrics Obviously lyrics can matter. A great lyric can make a song hit harder, and bad lyrics can ruin a song if they are distracting enough But I think people often talk about music as if the lyrics are the “real” substance and everything else is just decoration. To me, that misses most of what music actually is The melody, rhythm, vocal tone, production, dynamics, texture, atmosphere and structure usually do more emotional work than the literal words. A song can have very simple lyrics and still be powerful because of how it sounds. A song can also have clever lyrics and still be boring if the music underneath is flat I also think this is why some people dismiss pop, dance music, metal, shoegaze, electronic music or music in languages they do not understand. They judge it too much like written poetry and not enough like sound Lyrics are part of music, but they are not automatically the deepest or most important part Do you think lyrics are genuinely central to judging music, or do music fans overrate them because words are easier to analyse than sound?

text: Why did Declan Mckenna never hit the mainstream as an artist? I get that he made Brazil which was an absolute massive global megahit, but it seems like while that song has no shortage of fans, Declan Mckenna the artist himself deserves so many more. What Do You Think About the Car is a phenomenal album with some absolutely phenomenal and unbelievably catchy songs, my favorites being The Kids Don’t want to Come Home, Isombard, Why Do You feel so Down, and Paracetamol. These songs are relevant, catchy, and fun, but none of them came even close to the success of Brazil. Zeros, his second album is arguably even better. Almost every song on that album I‘d consider a masterpiece. Declan does what he did on his previous album but times a hundred. His third album, What Happened to the Beach is far less consistent or accessible but still has some great, easy to love tracks like Sympathy, Nothing Works, and Mulholland’s Dinner and Wine. Tl:dr Declan Mckenna has an extremely great discography full of phenomenal songs but doesn’t seem to get enough recognition for it
